[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The closing statement that God knows all deeds is a threat, although its wording can encompass promise as well as threat.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The trust clause conditionally binds the debtor to repay; the imperative is obligatory, supported by consensus, judicial enforcement, and sound reports forbidding appropriation of another’s property.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Athim qalbuhu describes the sin attaching to concealment; qalbuhu may be the subject of athim, the subject whose clause completes the predicate, or a partitive apposition.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Amānatihi can name the debt owed, called a trust because it is related to the debtor, or mean the trust itself, so the wording means to preserve one’s honor by repaying it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أحمد بن موسى | reports | He labels the raised-alif reading attributed to Abu Bakr from ʿĀṣim as the reading alladhī utumina.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أحمد بن موسى | rejects | He calls that reading label erroneous; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the standard form read by the other reciters is correct and alone permissible, while Abu ʿAlī defends Ahmad’s position.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · سليم عن حمزة | reports | Sulaym transmits an imāla-like rounding of the hamza to ḍamma in this word, which the author also calls impermissible.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو علي | prefers | Abu ʿAlī approves Ahmad ibn Musa’s entire reading position and argues in its favor, contrary to the author’s judgment.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Suppressing testimony is forbidden, as indicated by the threat; the duty applies when a witness fears a right will be lost.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عباس | reports | A witness should testify whenever summoned and inform the parties when asked, rather than reserving the information for a governor, so the wrongdoer may turn back.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p388/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Ibn ʿAṭiyya limits that advice by circumstances: under corrupt conditions, giving testimony in an ineffective venue may aid falsehood and conceal the truth.
[TABRISI:2:283#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن كثير وأبو عمرو | reports | Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read رهن as faʿl; the other readers read رهٰان on the faʿāl pattern.
[TABRISI:2:283#2/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī says رهن began as a verbal noun, became a noun by transfer, and is pluralized on both فعْل and فعال patterns; the cited verse attests the form.
[TABRISI:2:283#2/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The root رهن means placing property as security; a pledge may also be called a mortgage, with related alternative forms and expressions for advancing or maintaining food.
[TABRISI:2:283#2/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿī says the reading أرهنتهم مالكا in Ibn Hammām's verse is mistaken; the correct wording is وأرهنهم مالكا.
[TABRISI:2:283#2/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The Prophetic rule لا يغلق الرهن invalidates a condition that if the borrower does not redeem by a set date the collateral becomes the creditor's property.
[TABRISI:2:283#2/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | When debtors travel without a scribe or witnesses, a received pledge serves as security and is valid only upon possession, by consensus.
[TABRISI:2:283#2/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | If the creditor trusts the debtor without a written or pledged security, the debtor must fully repay at maturity without denial or delay.
[TABRISI:2:283#2/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The order not to conceal testimony addresses witnesses after they have borne it; intentional concealment by one who knows the fact and can testify without harm makes the heart sinful.
[TABRISI:2:283#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Sin is assigned to the heart because the decision to conceal is made there, and this wording intensifies blame; the verse on faith in hearts provides a parallel. | mentions 58:22
[TABRISI:2:283#3/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God knows what people conceal; a report from the Prophet says a false witness leaves the judge only after taking his seat in Hell, as does one who hides testimony.
[TABRISI:2:283#3/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The clause permitting trust between the parties shows that writing and witnesses in debt transactions are safeguards, not obligations.
[TABRISI:2:283#3/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The two verses show God's care in teaching people what they need for worldly and religious life, offering insight to the reflective.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p341#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Travel is singled out because writers and witnesses are less commonly available there; when written documentation is unavailable, take a pledge in hand.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p341#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and ʿAbd al-Warith read ruhun without alif; ʿAbd al-Warith also has a sukun for ease of pronunciation.

[RAZI-FULL:v7p104#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The passage distinguishes three transaction safeguards: writing with witnesses, taking a pledged security, and relying on trust; the pledge addresses travel when writing or writing tools are unavailable.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p104#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أهل اللغة | reports | The root of safar carries meanings of uncovering or clarification; al-Razi connects it with a book, travel that exposes character, emergence into open country, dawn, and sweeping away dust. | mentions 2:184
[RAZI-FULL:v7p104#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rahn derives from permanence and firmness; as a verbal noun it names something deposited as security and functions as a direct object.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p104#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A poetic line uses rāhin for pledged sons and illustrates the word’s use as deposited collateral.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأعشى | reports | Al-Asha uses rahn in a line about refusing to give sons as pledges, illustrating this plural form.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Jurists allow pledges both at home and while traveling; Mujahid limits them to travel, but al-Razi rejects that restriction because travel is the usual context, like fear in the prayer-shortening verse. | mentions 4:101
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعيث | reports | The poet Baith uses al-rahn for pledged property left with a woman, another example of the plural form.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says the pattern فعل and فعلى is rare, while the source compares alternations in words such as سقف and نشر.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra analyzes rahn as a plural of rihan and rihan as a plural of rahn, treating rahn as a plural of a plural.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Another group reverses the proposed relationship, taking rahn as the plural of rahn and rihan as the plural of rahn.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Razi rejects the disputed plural-of-plural accounts because the proposals cancel each other and Sibawayh does not treat that pattern as regular; he prefers rihan as the straightforward plural of rahn.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن كثير وأبو عمرو | reports | Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read فرهان with a damma on both letters, and a further report gives their reading with a still second syllable; Abu Amr distinguishes collateral from horse-racing stakes.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash criticizes Abu Amr reading rahan with a still second syllable because that plural pattern is rare and irregular, though he lists analogies.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p105/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The clause فرهان مقبوضة is elliptical: it can be an incomplete subject with an omitted predicate, or a predicate with الوثيقة understood as subject.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · القفال | reports | Al-Qaffal says that because a trusted debtor may turn out dishonest, God urges anyone who knows the transaction to help preserve the creditor’s right by testifying, whether or not the creditor knows of the testimony.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | A prophetic report supports Al-Qaffal’s reading: the best witness is one who testifies before being asked.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One interpretation takes concealing testimony to mean denying knowledge of the event, as in the denial concerning Abraham’s family in 2:140. | mentions 2:140
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Another interpretation is withholding testimony when needed; as already stated at 2:282, refusal can defeat a Muslim’s property right and is gravely warned against. | mentions 2:282
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عمر | reports | A report says ʿUmar taught a Bedouin that athīm in the phrase about the tree of Zaqqūm means a wicked person, not an orphan. | mentions 44:43, 44:44
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Kashshāf parses āthim as the predicate of inna and qalbuhu as its nominative agent, equivalent to saying that his heart sins.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A reading with qalbahu in the accusative parallels safiha nafsahu in 2:130. | mentions 2:130
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abī ʿAblah reads qalbuhu Allāh, explaining the construction as God making the heart sinful.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The jurists agree that pledges are valid both at home and on a journey, whether or not a writer is available; the travel condition is customary rather than restrictive. | mentions 4:101
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A pledge in jointly owned undivided property is invalid according to the cited argument: a pledge must be received, but an undivided share cannot be physically possessed.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | When the creditor trusts the debtor and takes no written record, witnesses, or pledge, the debtor must honor the trust and repay rather than deny the debt; the verse’s reference to trust means absence of fear of betrayal. | mentions 12:64
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | An alternative makes the trust-duty address the pledge-holder, who must return the pledge upon repayment, but al-Razi prefers the reading addressed to the debtor.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p106/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Razi rejects the claim that this verse abrogates the earlier safeguards: they are recommendations for prudent practice and this verse grants a concession; Ibn ʿAbbas likewise says the debt passage contains no abrogation. | mentions 2:282
[RAZI-FULL:v7p107/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · كثير من المتكلمين | reports | Many theologians argue that the heart is the acting, knowing, commanded, and prohibited subject; they infer this from God attributing sin to the heart here. | mentions 26:193
[RAZI-FULL:v7p107/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · من خالف في هذا القول | reports | Opponents answer that an act can be attributed to a body part because that organ supplies its chief enabling cause, as in saying the eye saw or ear heard.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p107/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Since bodily acts follow the heart’s motives and inclinations, the sin is attributed to the heart in this verse.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p107/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God’s complete knowledge of actions and inner thoughts warns against concealing testimony: the accountable person knows every deed will be judged and recompensed; the following verse is cited. | mentions 2:284
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#10/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Debt brings mental preoccupation, humiliation before creditors, and pressure that can lead to lying, broken promises, or broken oaths; these harms diminish its dignity.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#10/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet sought refuge from sin and debt because indebted people may lie when speaking and break promises.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#10/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A believer's soul remains pledged in the grave by an unpaid debt until someone pays it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#10/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The commands to document, witness, and take pledges decisively require safeguarding and developing wealth, against ascetics who give everything away and leave dependants to others' charity or oppression.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#10/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو الفرج الجوزي | rejects | Al-Jawzi condemns learned advocates of total divestment as opposing both reason and the law; he says al-Muhasibi and Abu Hamid al-Tusi reinforced that teaching.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#10/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · المحاسبي | reports | Al-Muhasibi recounts that some Companions feared for Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf because of his wealth, while Ka'b defended how he earned, spent, and left it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#11/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says the wealthy are few on Judgment Day, except those who give generously in both directions.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#11/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · المحاسبي | reports | Al-Muhasibi says Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf's lawful earnings delayed his entry with the poor, so he would crawl behind them toward Paradise.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#11/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حامد | reports | Abu Hamid argues that even charitable wealth distracts from remembering God, so an aspirant should retain only necessities and give away every sum that occupies the heart.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#11/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو الفرج الجوزي | rejects | Al-Jawzi answers that God dignified wealth as human sustenance, prohibited entrusting it to the foolish, and ordered its return when orphans attain sound judgment. | mentions 4:5, 4:6
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#11/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet told Sa'd that leaving heirs financially secure is better than leaving them needy and asking people for help.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#11/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet called sound wealth in the hands of a righteous person a good thing.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#11/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet said Abu Bakr's wealth benefited him and prayed for Anas to receive abundant, blessed wealth and children.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#11/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | When Ka'b offered to give away all his property as repentance, the Prophet told him to keep some beca

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#11/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو الفرج الجوزي | holds | Al-Jawzi acknowledges wealth's temptations but says lawful earnings are necessary; gathering more is judged by intent, and supporting one's family, poor people, and public good can make it better than many devotions.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#12/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet allotted land to al-Zubayr according to how far his horse ran and his whip reached, an example of permitting acquisition.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#12/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Desire for increase is natural: Sa'd ibn Ubada prayed for abundance, Joseph's brothers sought an extra camel-load, Shu'ayb offered Moses ten years, and Job gathered golden locusts. | mentions 12:65, 28:27
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#12/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | rejects | Al-Qurtubi calls al-Muhasibi's account of Abu Dharr confronting Ka'b impossible and fabricated; its claimed route through Ibn Lahi'a is unreliable, and Abu Dharr died seven years before Abd al-Rahman.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#12/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | rejects | The story's content is implausible: the Companions would not condemn wealth lawfully acquired, and it makes no sense that the law would permit and then punish it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#12/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | rejects | The crawling report about Abd al-Rahman is weak: its transmitter Ammara ibn Zadhan was criticized by al-Bukhari, Ahmad, Abu Hatim, and al-Daraqutni.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#12/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib says wealth is needed to repay debts and protect one's honor; he left four hundred dinars, while Sufyan al-Thawri called money a weapon in that era.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#12/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | Al-Qurtubi says soundly intended accumulation of lawful wealth is better than abandoning it; early Muslims praised and gathered it for emergencies and helping the poor, while some chose less to focus on worship.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#13/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet's declaration that one killed defending property is a martyr is further evidence that wealth must be protected; fuller discussion is promised in al-Ma'ida.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#13/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr, showing that property deserves protection.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#2/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمرو وابن كثير | reports | Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read rahun; other readings include ruhun and ruhan, with grammarians disputing whether these are plural forms or collective nouns.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#2/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · المهدوي | reports | Al-Mahdawī parses 'pledges' as a subject with an omitted predicate: possessed pledges suffice for security.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#2/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A pledge is property retained as security so a creditor can recover from its price or proceeds if collection from the debtor fails; the Arabic root also means permanence and continuity.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#2/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو علي الفارسي | reports | Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says the small plural of rahn is unattested; if it existed, its pattern would be afʿāl, as in kalb and aklab.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#3/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو علي وأبو زيد | reports | Abū ʿAlī and Abū Zayd distinguish forms of the pledge verb: arhantu is used for bidding high, while raḥantu is used for loans and sales.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#3/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الزجاج وابن الأعرابي والأخفش | reports | Al-Zajjāj, Ibn al-Aʿrābī, and al-Akhfash also allow both raḥantu and arhantu for pledging.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#3/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عبد الله بن همام السلولي | reports | A verse by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hammām al-Salūlī uses arhantu; most transmitters retain that form, while al-Aṣmaʿī reads a present-tense verb after the past and explains the wāw as circumstantial.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#3/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The pledged person is the one receiving the pledge; an object may be called marhūn or rahīn, a woman rahīna, and rahantu is standard for pledging in a sale or loan.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#3/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Qurṭubī adopts the view that a pledge ends if it voluntarily returns to the pledgor, following the requirement that it be possessed; Abū Ḥanīfa exempts return as a loan or deposit, while al-Shāfiʿī preserves the earlier possession.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#3/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī says a pledge made verbally but never physically possessed creates no legal effect, because the verse predicates the ruling on possession.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#3/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · المالكية | reports | The Mālikīs say the contract binds the pledgor and require delivery; possession completes the pledge's benefit, while two other schools make it a condition of bindingness and validity. | mentions 5:1, 17:34
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#4/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · المالكية | reports | The Mālikīs support the pledge's binding contract by commands to fulfill contracts and promises, and the Prophetic rule that believers fulfill their conditions. | mentions 5:1, 17:34
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#4/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · جمهور العلماء | prefers | Possession by a neutral custodian counts as receipt because the custodian represents the creditor; Ibn Abī Laylā, Qatāda, al-Ḥakam, and ʿAṭāʾ require the creditor to hold it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#4/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | If collateral with a neutral custodian is lost, neither creditor nor custodian is liable: the creditor never possessed it and the custodian is a trustee.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#4/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن المنذر | reports | Ibn al-Mundhir argues that a Ḥanafī exception allowing two creditors jointly to take a plot as collateral concedes that a share in common property may be pledged.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#4/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن المنذر | prefers | Ibn al-Mundhir considers pledging jointly owned property valid just as selling it is valid; al-Qurṭubī's school permits it against Abū Ḥanīfa's school.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#4/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The Mālikīs permit pledging a debt owed by another: anything saleable may be collateral, and a debt has value, though opponents say it cannot be physically possessed or directly realized.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#4/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو هريرة | reports | Al-Bukhārī transmits from Abū Hurayra the Prophet's rule that an animal pledged as collateral may be ridden and its milk drunk in return for the expense borne by the user.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#5/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الخطابي | reports | Al-Khaṭṭābī says the first wording does not identify whether the pledgor, creditor, or custodian may ride and milk the pledged animal.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#5/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أحمد وإسحاق | reports | A more explicit Abū Hurayra report says the creditor who feeds a pledged animal may ride or drink its milk in proportion to the expense; Aḥmad and Isḥāq adopt that rule.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:283#5/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو ثور | reports | Abū Thawr permits a creditor who maintained neglected collateral to ride it or use an enslaved servant; al-Awzāʿī and al-Layth share this view.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p550/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Witnesses must not conceal testimony, whether or not the claimant already knows it; greed, fear, or hope can otherwise silence them and create conflict.

[ALUSI-FULL:v3p62/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الجمهور | reports | The majority require the pledge to be physically delivered to complete it.

[ALUSI-FULL:v3p62/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو علي | reports | Abu Ali’s verse uses rahin for bread and meat as things still held or remaining, illustrating the pledge’s implication of continuity.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | God repays each person according to the conduct at issue: good is repaid with good and evil with evil.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Do not conceal testimony by refusing to give it when summoned; the address is to believing witnesses, as transmitted from early authorities.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abi ʿAbla reads āthama qalbahu, making the heart sinful.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | God knows whether people conceal testimony or deliver it properly and will repay them accordingly.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿid ibn Jubayr and others are cited for reading the command as addressed to witnesses.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | An alternative address to debtors, meaning they should acknowledge debt or avoid defeating witnesses in court, conflicts with the apparent wording and early transmitted interpretation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A variant reads the verb for concealing in the third-person plural.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The pronoun in innahu most naturally returns to whoever conceals testimony; some make it a pronoun of the matter, though a following participial phrase is not a sentence for Basran and Kufan grammarians.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Grammarians parse āthim as predicate with qalb as its subject, as predicate before a delayed subject, or with qalb in apposition; al-Farra and al-Akhfash also allow qalb as the subject of āthim, a construction most grammarians reject.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Attributing the sin to the heart is concise because concealment is an inward act; naming the chief organ intensifies the warning and shows the enormity of the sin.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Alusi dismisses additional explanations that the attribution alludes to a black mark from sin or to the heart’s effect on the whole body.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p63/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A variant puts qalb in the accusative by analogy with an object; Abu Hayyan permits it as partitive apposition, while some call it specification and Abu al-Baqa rejects that.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A pledge is the recourse when traveling and no scribe is available, but these conditions concern resort to collateral, not its validity or permissibility.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | It is permissible for parties to dispense with all three securities and rely wholly on mutual trust; the trusted debtor must repay the trust.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Permission to rely on trust shows that writing, witnessing, and pledging are recommendations rather than obligations; otherwise this permission would abrogate the prior commands.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Hasan, Şa‘bî, Hakem b. Uteybe | reports | Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, and al-Hakam b. Utayba are among exegetes who say this verse abrogates the earlier instructions.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Ibn Abbas explicitly says the debt verse is not abrogated but remains decisive; with no proof that this verse came later, most exegetes agree there is no abrogation.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Most exegetes treat permission to rely on trust as evidence that the securities are recommended; ʿAta, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Nakhaʿi instead make the pledge recommended while treating feasible writing and witnessing as obligatory.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Abu Bakr al-Razi’s account in Ahkam al-Qur’an says the juristic position is recommendation.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Whatever the status of the safeguards, the person entrusted with property is obligated to discharge the trust fully and must fear God rather than misuse the trust.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Witnesses must neither refuse to testify when needed nor conceal known truth; debtors likewise must not deny a debt they know and have witnessed.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Concealing testimony is a grave inward sin of the heart, the locus of faith, and approaches unbelief or lack of creed.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r19] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Ibn Abbas counts associating partners with God, false testimony, and concealing testimony among the greatest major sins.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verse’s travel-and-no-scribe condition cannot be inverted to forbid pledges when one is resident or a scribe is available; the lack of a scribe makes writing impossible.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r20] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God knows every hidden and manifest act, including giving or concealing testimony, and will punish accordingly.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Travel is the customary or usual cause of lacking a scribe, not a restrictive condition; the same rule applies to another excuse that prevents finding a

[ELMALILI:2:283/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A pledge is permissible while resident too, as shown by the Prophet pledging his coat of mail in a settled state.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | When writing can secure a debt, requesting a pledge between believers is permissible but not recommended unless there is an excuse.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Taking possession is required to complete a pledge; an unpossessed pledge gives no security, and an undivided fractional share cannot properly be pledged.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Writing, witnessing, and pledging are the three means of securing debts and transactions; faith and piety should encourage these protections of people’s rights and lawful wealth.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Securing lawful wealth enables lawful earning and spending in God’s path and helps avoid usury and similar sins so that piety can continue.
[ELMALILI:2:283/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The strongest assurance for human rights is obedience to God through faith and piety; without it, secondary safeguards have limited benefit.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p105/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The next verse gives pledge as the alternative when a writer cannot be found, without making unwritten testimony an intermediate option; thus a writer may also be one of the witnesses. | mentions 2:283
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p120/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Writing and testimony rules apply in ordinary settled conditions when available; when travel prevents finding someone to write or witness, a pledge supplies the final transactional arrangement, extended to similar circumstances.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p120/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Rihān is a plural of rahn, also pluralized as ruhan; the majority of the ten readers vocalize it with kasra then fatḥa, while Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr use ḍamma on both letters.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p120/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Rahn names the pledged object by its verbal noun; the debtor places property in the creditor’s possession as security, and the root means detention, as in the verse about every soul held by its deeds. | mentions 74:38
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p120/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Zuhayr’s line uses a pledge that cannot be released as an image of a debt secured by property held until payment.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p120/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Pre-Islamic Arabs commonly pledged property for guarantees and blood-money, sometimes even sons or prominent men as hostages.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p120/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الأعشى | reports | Al-Aʿshā’s poem recalls Kisrā seeking children as hostages, which the speaker vowed not to provide lest they be corrupted.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p120/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عبد الله بن همام السلولي | reports | ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hammām al-Sulūlī’s verse describes escaping danger while leaving Mālik as a hostage.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p120/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · كعب بن الأشرف | reports | Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf asked ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf to pledge his sons as hostages.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p122/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | If the parties trust one another, the creditor is the one trusting and the debtor is the one trusted with the creditor’s property or right.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p122/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Amāna derives from giving security; it can name the trusted property itself, and its possessive construction resembles a verbal noun joined to its object.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p122/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Calling a debt or pledge an amāna gives the right gravity: failing to return it is betrayal, and a Prophetic report commands returning deposits without reciprocating betrayal.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p122/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet commands returning a trust to its owner and not betraying someone even if that person betrayed you.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p122/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Performance means payment or fulfillment, return of the thing itself or its equivalent when fungible, and not denying the debt, as in the command to return trusts to their owners. | mentions 4:58
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p122/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | For the majority who treat debt documentation as recommended, this trust provision completes the guidance: parties may document and witness, or rely on their known honesty. | mentions 2:282
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p123/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The trust clause is followed by a charge to both parties to fulfill what they owe and fear God.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p123/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbī, Ibn Jurayj, Jābir ibn Zayd, al-Rabīʿ ibn Sulaymān, and an attribution to Abū Saʿīd say mutual trust abrogated the earlier duty to write and witness debts. | mentions 2:282
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p123/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | If Abū Saʿīd’s position is sound, the author says their term abrogation uses an older sense meaning specification of general circumstances or times.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p123/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الطبري | reports | Those who retain obligatory writing and testimony, including al-Ṭabarī, confine the trust clause to the travel-pledge case; the author says al-Ṭabarī’s explanation is unclear.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p123/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | The author suggests this narrow view could mean that travelers lacking a pledge may proceed only if they trust each other, though its adherents do not clearly state this and may omit it to encourage mutual generosity.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p123/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | The author prefers an independent rule covering every debt setting and transaction: testimony, pledge, repayment, and sale; the undefined baʿḍ includes trust from either direction.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p123/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A creditor trusts a debtor by dispensing with witnesses and a pledge; a debtor trusts a creditor by giving a pledge worth more than the debt, so each must honor the other’s entrusted right.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p123/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The debtor must repay without delay or denial; the creditor holding an overvalued pledge must return it without denial or withholding any part, since the collateral exceeds the debt.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p124/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Amāna refers both to the quality of being trustworthy and to the entrusted object.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p124/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The author rejects pre-Islamic foreclosure, by which the creditor became owner of a pledge after nonpayment at the deadline; the Prophet forbade a pledge from being closed off in this way.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p124/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says that a pledge is not forfeited to the creditor.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p124/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Zuhayr’s verse reflects the old practice of a pledge becoming locked and irredeemable.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p124/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Mutual trust means both parties say they need no witnesses because each trusts the other; this avoids reviving suspicion between debtors and creditors.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p124/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Repeating God’s name before the command to fear Him adds solemn awe even though a pronoun could have been used.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The general ban on concealing testimony is a second charge to witnesses, summarizing the commands to write justly and not refuse testimony. | mentions 2:282
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A prohibition repeats whenever the occasion to commit the act arises; witnesses should disclose what they know whenever needed and may act earlier if absence, forgetfulness, or death could erase the evidence.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The earlier commands to make testimony clear and to accept an invitation show the law’s concern to reveal rights, not suppress them. | mentions 2:282
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet calls the best witnesses those who bring their testimony before being asked; Mālik records it, and Muslim and the four Sunan collections transmit it from him.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125#2/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The author says this interpretation is supported by both transmitted evidence and reasoning.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125#2/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a sound report from Abū Hurayra, the Prophet praises the earliest generations and then warns of later people who testify before being asked.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | The majority retain the hamza in alladhī ʾūtumina after the connecting hamza drops, since there is then no reason to change it into a long vowel.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ورش | reports | Warsh from Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and Abū Jaʿfar read al-ladhītumina, changing the hamza to wāw under the passive-form vowel and then wāw to yāʾ after the connecting hamza drops.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو بكر عن عاصم | reports | Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim reads alladhī awtumin, using wāw to represent the hamza following a ḍamma.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p125/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | These recitational differences concern oral delivery and do not conflict with the written consonantal text.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p128/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Calling the concealer’s heart sinful attributes the act to

the mental faculty that intends it; the heart signifies perception, emotion, and intention, which causes the committed sin. | mentions 7:116
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p128/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The verse about concealing testimony threatens punishment: because only ignorance could prevent a capable God from requiting action, divine knowledge implies judgment.
[TABATABAI:2:282-283/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | He defines the key terms: mutual debt, dictation, shortchanging, weariness, causing harm, disobedience, and the two plural forms for pledged collateral.
[TABATABAI:2:282-283/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The two verses contain nearly twenty legal rulings, including rules for debt and pledges; detailed legal debate belongs in jurisprudence, so he leaves it aside here.
[ASAD-NOTES:2:283#n276/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The ban on concealing testimony covers transaction witnesses and a debtor who accepted a trust-based loan without writing or witnesses and later denies the debt.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:283/r1] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Collateral is a material asset taken from the debtor and convertible to payment; Islam forbids using a human being as collateral, despite pre-Islamic practices that sometimes pledged children.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:283/r2] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | When travel makes a scribe hard to find, a suitable pledge can replace writing; the Prophet's practice shows pledges are allowed outside travel as well.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:283/r3] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Hanefî ve Şâfiîler | reports | Hanafis and Shafiis say a pledge contract is invalid if the collateral has not been taken out of the debtor's control; Malik says it is valid but binding only upon delivery, and the debtor can be compelled to deliver it.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:283/r4] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | A creditor may not benefit from property pledged as security for a debt.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:283/r5] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | reports | Among jurists who consider writing, dictation, and witnesses obligatory, some take the mutual-trust clause to lift that obligation, while others limit pledges as a substitute to travel; those who see security as recommended view the clause as reinforcing that advice.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:283/r6] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · İbn Âşûr | prefers | Ibn Ashur's wider reading, which the author endorses, extends fidelity to trust across all debt relations; without trust and responsibility, parties can wrong one another even when security exists.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:283/r7] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Those who know relevant testimony may not conceal it; they should come forward even if not asked, while hadiths criticizing unsolicited testimony are understood as concerning God's rights or false testimony.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:283/r8] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Concealing testimony is a sin of the mind and will rather than an outward bodily act, which explains calling the heart sinful.
[QIRAAT-ER:2:283:11#1/r1] QIRAAT-ER · author | reports | Ruhun and rihān are both canonical plurals of rahn: the former is broken and the latter sound.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p149/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · روح المعاني | reports | Rūḥ al-Maʿānī defines guardianship as preservation and rectification, noting that the root originally referred to protecting livestock by feeding it or warding off predators. | mentions 23:8, 70:32
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p149/r2] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | The author says riyāʿa is broader than mere preservation: it includes care, correction, stewardship, and monitoring, all needed to discharge a trust.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p149/r3] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | A trusted guardian must attend to dependents’ needs, a ruler must oversee subjects, and one entrusted with crops, livestock, or religious obligations must actively discharge the charge and seek what pleases God.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p149/r4] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Unlike chastity, which remains with the person, trusts may be remote or hidden from view and exposed to thieves, so the trustee must inspect and tend them like a shepherd; riyāʿa is the apt term. | mentions 23:5-7, 70:29-31
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p149/r5] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | The nominal form raaʿūn, rather than the verb yarʿawn, signals that this guardianship must remain constant and never lapse. | mentions 23:8, 70:32
[STUDYQURAN:2:283/r1] STUDYQURAN · Q, Ṭ | reports | Not finding a scribe can mean lacking the means to write the contract.
[STUDYQURAN:2:283/r2] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | A pledge is collateral given by a debtor to a creditor or by a forward-sale seller to a buyer as security without a written contract and witnesses.
[STUDYQURAN:2:283/r3] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The verse allows the parties to trust one another without taking property as a pledge.
[STUDYQURAN:2:283/r4] STUDYQURAN · Q, R, Ṭ | reports | Some say the trust provision abrogates 2:282’s contract rules; many restrict it to travel and retain written contracts as the ordinary rule. | mentions 2:282
